chain: Sulfur supplied to skin and hair
methylsulfonylmethane-msm.text: Users take MSM in the hope of softer, lighter skin, stronger hair and nails, and joints that stay comfortable for training. Forum posters also claim it lightens eye colour and preserves height through the day. A few small skin trials exist; the other claims rest on anecdote.

chain: Blocks an enzyme in fat synthesis
hydroxycitric-acid-hca.text: HCA from Garcinia cambogia is promoted as a fat blocker that users take to get leaner. The mechanism comes from lab enzyme data, and human trials have measured weight change rather than visible leanness, with small short-term differences reported.

hydroxycut.text: Hydroxycut is a mass-market caffeine-based fat burner that people use during cutting phases to get leaner. Current formulas centre on caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee. Evidence for the branded products specifically comes mostly from manufacturer-linked studies.

dexatrim.text: Dexatrim is a long-running diet-pill brand used as an appetite suppressant and energy aid for losing weight. Current versions are caffeine and green-tea blends. The brand's own products have little trial evidence for fat loss, though its ingredients are studied individually.

cortislim.text: CortiSlim was marketed to people wanting to lose weight, especially around the midsection, by controlling cortisol. The idea that supplements can trim stress-related belly fat is a marketing theory; no published trials test the product, and its advertising drew an FTC action.

metabolife.text: Metabolife 356 was the best-selling fat burner of its era, taken by people dieting for a leaner look. Its ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss. It is documented here mainly as a historical example after the federal ephedra ban.

chromium-nicotinate.text: Chromium nicotinate is taken for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control, on the idea that chromium improves how the body handles carbohydrate. Trials of chromium forms have measured body composition directly, with mixed results.

policosanol.text: Policosanol is a sugarcane-wax supplement used for cholesterol, and it is listed on the wiki among metabolism-related products. Users who include it in fat-loss stacks do so through the general-health link. Lipid results are debated, and no studies address body fat or appearance.

red-yeast-rice.text: Red yeast rice is taken for cholesterol and appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the body healthy over decades. Its cholesterol effect is studied; it is not used for a direct appearance outcome.

fucoidan.text: Fucoidan is sold in longevity circles as a seaweed extract for healthy ageing and skin. Most findings come from cell and animal studies on inflammation and skin biology; human trials on appearance have not been run.

cycloastragenol.text: Cycloastragenol is marketed as a telomerase activator for slowing ageing, which users hope shows up as a younger look. Support comes from cell and animal work. No trials have tested its effect on appearance.

chain: Tonic herb for immunity and vitality
astragalus.text: Astragalus root (huangqi) is a classic Chinese tonic taken as an immune and anti-ageing herb, and longevity enthusiasts include it in stacks aimed at ageing well. Its use is traditional and general; no appearance trials exist.

gynostemma-pentaphyllum-jiaogulan.text: Jiaogulan tea and extracts are used as a ginseng-like adaptogen in longevity routines. Users link general health and stress resilience with ageing well. Evidence is mostly lab-based with thin human data and no appearance trials.

schisandra-chinensis.text: Schisandra berry extract is taken as an adaptogen in longevity circles, valued for antioxidant and liver-support properties. The link to looks is general healthy ageing. Studies are mainly lab-based on the liver and antioxidants, with nothing on appearance.

rhodiola-rosea.text: Rhodiola is taken as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue, so users can stay energised and recover, and some posters discuss effects on testosterone and estrogen. Human trials on fatigue are of mixed quality; its appearance use is untested.

eleutherococcus-siberian-ginseng.text: Eleuthero is used as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue, with some users believing a calmer stress response shows in their skin and general look. Human evidence on stress is thin, and the appearance link is based on anecdote.

rhaponticum-carthamoides-maral-root.text: Maral root is sold to lifters as an ecdysteroid-rich herb to build muscle and speed recovery, and is also used as an adaptogen. Muscle claims rest on animal data and anecdote; no human trial of the herb supports them.

ganoderma-lucidum-reishi-lingzhi.text: Reishi is taken as tea or extract for immunity, stress and sleep, with users hoping better rest improves how they look. Clinical evidence for sleep and immunity is limited, and nothing tests it for appearance directly.

royal-jelly.text: Royal jelly is taken as a supplement and used in cosmetics for skin quality and a youthful look. EFSA reviewed the human health claims and found no support, and no trial covers appearance.

chain: Less oxidative skin damage, melasma support
maritime-pine-bark-extract-pycnogenol.text: Pycnogenol is taken as an antioxidant for skin elasticity, hydration and melasma. The link to skin biology is plausible from lab work. Cochrane found insufficient evidence for other uses, and no skin trial was identified.

grape-seed-extract.text: Grape seed extract is taken as a polyphenol antioxidant for skin and ageing, and some forum posters use it as a claimed aromatase inhibitor to lower estrogen. The appearance case rests on lab data; no trials test skin or looks.

genistein.text: Genistein is a soy isoflavone that users consider for skin ageing, since phytoestrogens act on estrogen receptors in skin. It has been studied for many conditions, but trials have not tested it for skin or looks.

diosmin.text: Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling, and some users try it hoping to reduce fluid retention and puffiness elsewhere, including the face. Its use for venous swelling is studied; face puffiness is untested.

krill-oil.text: Krill oil is taken as a phospholipid-bound omega-3 source with astaxanthin, for skin and general health. It raises blood EPA and DHA in studies, but effects on skin and looks have not been tested.

sodium-beta-hydroxybutyrate-bhb-salts.text: BHB salts are used by people on low-carb diets who hope raised ketones help with appetite and fat loss. They do raise blood BHB; effects on fat loss or looks have not been tested.

ketone-monoester-r-1-3-butanediol-ester.text: The ketone monoester drink is used to raise blood ketones quickly, with fat loss and appetite control as the appearance interest. One study found lower appetite hormones; fat-loss results are unpublished.

glyceryl-tris-3-hydroxybutyrate.text: This ketone triglyceride (3GHB) is discussed in ketone-supplement circles as a way to raise BHB, with fat loss as the hoped-for outcome. Human work so far is limited to pharmacokinetic studies.

r-1-3-butanediol.text: R-1,3-butanediol is used in the ketone-supplement field as a precursor that raises blood ketones, with fat loss as the hoped-for outcome. Human evidence for appearance or fat loss is not established.

alanyl-glutamine.text: Alanyl-glutamine is a stable glutamine dipeptide that some lifters consider for muscle recovery and retention. Its research is in hospital nutrition, such as muscle glutamine loss after surgery; no trials target physique or appearance.

chain: Supplies muscle's main free amino acid
glutamine.text: Glutamine is taken by lifters as a recovery supplement so they can train harder and build more muscle. Its clinical evidence is in medical settings such as illness and injury, not physique.
